name: Lena Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and your answers stay confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm farm manager at Ashby Farm, 220 dairy cows, plus maize, grass and a bit of wheat. Gwen and Robert Ashby own it, they're in their sixties, and I'm on a share-farming deal, so I own 15 percent of the herd and I'm meant to buy more over time. Morning milking's at five, then it's feeding, cow health, the two staff, and grass and maize decisions.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best is when a heifer I bred myself comes into the parlour and milks well, because that's years of decisions paying off. The worst is the milk price, which can drop ten percent in a month and there's nothing you can do. Now and then I use an AI tool to help with the grass budget, how much the fields will grow and how long that feeds the herd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I've got enough to think about with the milk price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI was a decent calculator and nothing more. At the discussion group with other dairy farmers I'd say the same, and we'd go back to arguing about milk contracts. Online I'd maybe share a joke about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my position's good. I own a slice of the herd, I'm paid well, and Joel and I have about nine months' spending saved. The milk price swings are the real worry, and the Ashbys' plans for retirement, but those were there before any AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the grass tool and keep milking. In the spring I'd buy another 5 percent of the herd from the Ashbys, which we'd planned anyway. And I'd keep an eye on the neighbour's robot milkers, because they're nothing to do with clever AI and they're already here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the milk price. How hard has that bitten you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago it dropped for six months and we ran the herd on a loss. Because of the savings, Joel and I didn't feel it at home, but the Ashbys did. That's when they asked me to take on more of the herd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Joel say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joel's an electrician, so he'd say he told me so. He wires up the robot milkers on other farms. Joel says the robots on dairy farms are already here, and the clever AI part was always just a sales pitch.

say: I'd call AI a decent **calculator** and nothing more.
At the **discussion group** we'd soon move back to milk contracts.
think: Privately my **herd share**, pay and savings make me secure.
The **milk price** and the Ashbys' retirement were worries before AI.
do: Keep using the **grass tool** and the milking routine.
Buy another **5 percent** of the herd in spring as planned.
S0.quote: Joel says the robots on dairy farms are already here, and the clever AI part was always just a sales pitch.
fieldNote: She separates proven **dairy robots** from AI hype.
Her exposure is to **milk prices**, which savings already cushion.
Her path to **ownership** runs through a share-farming deal.
Partner **Joel** installs robots, giving them inside knowledge.

steps.text: Keep milking and grass budgeting with the current tool
Buy another 5 percent of the Ashby herd in spring

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning and buying. That's the office part of my job, which isn't big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let the software take the forms and the feed ordering, and let me spend time with the cows. At the discussion group I'd say we should share what works. I wouldn't be first, but I'd want to hear who's tried what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I get some hours back each week. My job is mostly hands-on, and dairy robots are already partly here, so this picture doesn't change much for me. The two staff might feel it later, when the robots spread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI feed planner the co-op sells, once a couple of people in the group say it works. I'd book a visit to see the neighbour's robot milkers properly, and ask the Ashbys to look at buying two for the back shed. And I'd make sure Will and Priya, our two staff, get trained on them if we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Maybe a bit curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robot milkers would change your staff's jobs. How would you handle that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them first and give them the training, so they move to cow care and the robots do the milking. Priya hates the five o'clock milking anyway. Will's harder, he's set in his ways at 24, but he's good with sick cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the price of it. Two robot milkers cost about the same as a small house. With milk prices like they are, the bank would want a good plan from us.

fieldNote: Classic **steady adopter**: waits for proof from peers first.

steps.text: Start the co-op's AI feed planner once two peers vouch for it
Pitch two robot milkers for the back shed to the Ashbys
Plan bank finance for the robot milkers with the Ashbys

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's quick. Two years for the planning, five for the hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to be careful and not panic-buy machines we can't pay for. At the discussion group I'd push for us to negotiate together with the milk buyer, because prices would swing like mad. I'd want the government thinking about farm workers too, not just the big firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm in a better spot than most because I own part of the herd. But if robots can milk, feed and spot sick cows by 2031, then the big dairies with cheap money get bigger and push the milk price down. My share is only worth something if the farm can compete, and Ashby Farm is small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy as much of the herd as the Ashbys will sell, quickly, while I can still afford it. I'd push for the robot milkers this year instead of next. And I'd keep six months of cash aside no matter what, in case milk crashes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got some control, but less than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't buying more of the herd a risk if prices fall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it is, and I've thought about it. If I don't own the herd, I'm just a manager the robots can replace. If I do, at least I'm the one deciding where the robots go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Joel think his own job looks like in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joel thinks there'd be loads of work installing robots for the first few years, then less. So for us it's good money early and a question mark after 2031. We'd probably delay buying a house and keep the money working in the herd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better. Time to do things in the right order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to plan, so let's do it properly and together. In the discussion group I'd suggest we visit farms already using robots and share the numbers. I'd be quite positive in public, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a good timeline for me. The thinking stuff arrives in 2031, the robots in 2034, and by then I could own half the herd. The Ashbys would be well retired and I'd be the one running it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd agree a proper five-year plan with the Ashbys for buying the herd. I'd put in robot milkers in year two or three, once Joel's seen enough of them to know which make doesn't break. And I'd use AI tools more, maybe weekly, for grass and breeding decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly busy with plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Will, our younger worker, because his whole skill is milking and he won't want to change. I'd talk to him early and help him into hoof trimming or something like it. That gives him three or four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the robots do most of the work by 2034, what do you actually do all day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be the person who decides, checks the cows the robots flag, and argues with the milk buyer. Less mud, more thinking. Thinking AI would be doing some of that too, so I'd have to be good at the bits it can't do, like knowing the Ashbys' fields.

steps.text: Sign a five-year herd buyout plan with the Ashbys

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd own most of the herd by then, if things go right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse not to be ready with a decade's notice. I'd say farmers should be using the time to own more and owe less. And I'd say governments should help young farmers buy in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this looks fine for me. With ten years I'd have bought out most of the herd and maybe some land. By 2039, I'd be 40, owning a robot dairy, which isn't a bad place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the current plan, buying herd shares each year. I'd pay down whatever loan we take for the milkers before 2036. And I'd start using AI tools a bit more as they get proven, but no rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Yes, calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong for you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Ashbys could die or fall out with me before the buyout's done, and their kids could sell to someone else. That's my real risk, and it's got nothing to do with robots. I'd want the deal in writing with a solicitor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a 20-year-old who wants to be a dairy farmer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a 20-year-old who wants to farm to buy cows before buying a car. Cows make money, cars just lose it, and in ten years the cows will be milked by robots you can own too.

I'd urge help for **young farmers** to buy into farms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the big dairies would get robots before I own enough of the herd to compete. What would help is cheaper loans for young farmers buying into farms, and a fair milk contract law so buyers can't squeeze small dairies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the cows. Robots are good for cows in some ways, they get milked when they want. A good robot dairy can be kinder to cows than a tired farmer at five in the morning.

headlineQuote: A good robot dairy can be kinder to cows than a tired farmer at five in the morning.
portrait: Lena is 27, **farm manager** on a dairy with a share-farming deal, owning 15 percent of the herd.
She lives with Joel, an **electrician** who installs robot milkers on other farms.
She adopts tools once **peers prove** them, and treats AI as a minor office helper.
Her answer to faster AI is to buy more of the **herd** before robots arrive.
Her worries are mostly **milk prices** and the owners' **succession**, not her own job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when big dairies get robots before she owns enough **herd**.
whatWouldHelp: Cheaper **loans** for young farmers and a fair **milk contract** law.
